source.title_on_document: Sketching vs. AI Prompt Based Design Intent Evolution in Undergraduate Students: an Exploratory Study

supplement.where: The paper refers to no supplementary material or online appendix.

paper_design_summary: 61 eighth-semester industrial design students at UNAM (Mexico City), in four student groups, were randomly assigned by group to two conditions: sketching with pen and paper (groups A+C, n=31) or free use of LLM and text-to-image tools of their choice (groups B+D, n=30). Each student worked individually for about one hour on a design brief about promoting conscious water use at home. Three design professors rated the creativity of each image-level idea (sketch or AI image plus text) on a 1-5 CAT scale, and the authors counted ideas, idea categories, and recurring concepts.

studies.label: Design task: sketching vs. generative AI (water-saving concept design)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Four intact student groups were randomly assigned to two conditions: sketch (groups A and C) or AI (groups B and D). Assignment was by group, not by individual; two groups per condition.
assignment.quote: the design task was carried out with four student groups, randomly assigned to two predefined conditions: sketch groups A+C (n=31) and AI groups B+D (n=30).
assignment.locator: p. 4, Section 3.2.2; group structure in p. 3, Figure 1

arms.name: Sketch (groups A+C)
arms.description: Pen and paper only; no devices allowed. Students photographed sketches and annotations.

arms.name: AI (groups B+D)
arms.description: Own laptops or smartphones; free use of AI tools of their choice (LLMs such as ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Copilot; text-to-image tools such as Krea.AI, Leonardo.AI). Students uploaded conversations and image results.

participants.exclusions: No exclusion of students is reported for the creativity rating: ideas from 31 sketch students and 30 AI students were rated (p. 4, Section 3.2.3). At the idea level, only ideas developed to image level with an explanatory description were rated, and AI images that were too abstract or discarded by students were dropped (number of dropped images not given). For the thematic prompt analysis, 3 of 30 AI logs were discarded and 27 analyzed (p. 10, Section 4.2.6). The diagnostic questionnaire was optional and answered by 42 (p. 5, Section 4.1).
participants.who: Industrial design bachelor students in their 8th semester (4th of 5 years); 38 female, 23 male; ages 21-30 (mean 22); recruited through a creative workshop in a regular mandatory course
participants.quote: The study involved 61 industrial design bachelor students in their 8th semester, which is the 4th year of a total of 5 years of design studies. Of these, 38 were female and 23 were male

ai_tool.name_model: Students' choice. LLMs: ChatGPT GPT-4o free (n=23), GPT-4o Plus (n=2), DeepSeek-R1 (n=3), Copilot (n=3), Gemini 2.5 (n=1). Text-to-image: Leonardo.AI Phoenix (n=15), Krea.AI Krea 1 (n=8), Meshy.AI (n=2), Vizcom (n=2), PromeAI (n=1), ArtGuru (n=1), GenCraft (n=1).
ai_tool.how_used: Free use of chatbots for ideation and of text-to-image tools for concept images; 28 of 30 AI students generated images from a prompt that the LLM wrote (pp. 8-9, Section 4.2.5). No prior prompting training (p. 12, Section 5.4).

task.description: Individual open-ended product design brief: 'how can we promote conscious water use in the home by its inhabitants?' Generate various ideas and detail a few of them, with sketches (sketch arm) or AI text and images (AI arm).
task.duration: About 1.5 hours in total: 30 minutes for explanation and documentation, 1 hour for the creative exercise (p. 4, Section 3.2.2)

outcomes.name: Expert CAT creativity rating of image-level ideas (sketch or AI image plus explanatory text)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Consensual Assessment Technique, 1-5 scale (1=not creative, 5=highly creative), three design professors with 10+ years of experience; two rating rounds (second in reverse order); ICC (two-way random, consistency) = 0.67, 95% CI 0.55-0.76. Table 1 also reports medians and the share of ideas in four score ranges. Multiple AI image variations of one idea counted as one concept.

contrasts.reported: Mean score per idea: sketch 2.52 (n=71 ideas) vs AI 2.89 (n=44 ideas); median 2.67 vs 3.00; low range (1-1.9) 18.3% vs 9.1%; medium (2.0-2.99) 52.1% vs 29.5%; medium-high (3-3.99) 26.8% vs 54.5%; high (4-5) 2.8% vs 6.8%. No SD, test, or interval for the pooled arm comparison.

contrasts.treatment_arm: AI group labelled 'Group C' in Section 4.2.1
contrasts.control_arm: Sketch group labelled 'Group A' in Section 4.2.1
contrasts.reported: Group A (Sketch, n = 54, M = 2.36, SD = 0.61) vs. Group C (AI, n = 24, M = 2.94, SD = 0.58); t(76) = -3.995, p < .001; d = 0.60, 95% CI [-0.98, -0.47]. n are ideas, not students.

contrasts.treatment_arm: AI group labelled 'Group D' in Section 4.2.1
contrasts.control_arm: Sketch group labelled 'Group B' in Section 4.2.1
contrasts.reported: Group B (Sketch, n = 17, M = 3.04, SD = 0.62) and Group D (AI, n = 20, M = 2.82, SD = 0.68); t(34.8) = 1.039, p = .306. n are ideas, not students.

outcomes.name: Homogenization: share of AI students producing the same concept (shower or faucet with a color-changing light ring)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Authors' qualitative review of image-level concepts; one recurring concept counted across AI students. The sketch arm is described only qualitatively as showing more diversity tied to local context (p. 7, Section 4.2.3).

contrasts.reported: light-ring shower/faucet concept: 18 out of 30 students (60%) in AI groups; no matching count for sketch groups. Direction coded for diversity (AI less diverse; the paper reports homogenization).
contrasts.locator: p. 6, Section 4.2.2; p. 7, Figure 4 and Section 4.2.3

diversity_detail.metric: Count and share of participants in a condition whose concepts share one recurring idea
diversity_detail.computed_over: Image-level concepts of all AI-arm students, hand-reviewed by the authors
diversity_detail.notes: Qualitative homogenization claim; sketch arm has no comparable statistic.

outcomes.name: Fluency at total idea level (written ideas and sketches vs LLM text ideas and TTI images)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of all ideas per participant, including text-level ideas; one AI participant produced 41 ideas at text level.

contrasts.reported: 89 total ideas by the sketch groups and 291 ideas for the AI groups; mean for AI is 9.7 ideas per participant and 2.8 for sketching. No SD or test.

outcomes.name: Fluency at image level (sketches vs AI images with description)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of image-level ideas per participant (the ideas rated in S1-O1).

contrasts.reported: 31 students generated 71 ideas based on sketches, and 30 students generated 44 ideas with AI on an image level; average of 2.2 ideas per participant with sketches vs 1.4 in the AI group. No SD or test.

outcomes.name: Idea categories explored per student (total idea level)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Each participant's total ideas sorted by hand into 12 categories (A-L) by focus or framing of the problem; average number of categories per student.

contrasts.reported: AI groups (B+D) present more categories than sketch groups (A+C), with an average of 4,2 versus 2 categories explored per student. No SD or test.

outcomes.name: Idea categories covered by each condition's pooled ideas (Figure 5 bubble charts)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Counts of total ideas per category (A-L) pooled over all students in a condition. Figure 5 shows idea counts by category; categories J, K, L (awareness campaigns, habit change, gamification/education) appear only in the AI groups.

contrasts.reported: Figure 5 bubble counts. Sketch: A 16, B 26, C 2, D 29, E 6, F 5, G 3, H 1, I 1 (no J-L). AI: A 83, B 39, C 2, D 59, E 9, F 4, G 3, H 5, I 4, J 30, K 22, L 31. Caption: 'The AI chart shows a greater number of explored categories'. Read from the figure; category-to-bubble assignment follows the branch labels.

diversity_detail.metric: Number of hand-coded idea categories covered by a condition's pooled ideas, and idea counts per category
diversity_detail.computed_over: All total-level ideas of all students in a condition, pooled (89 sketch, 291 AI)
diversity_detail.notes: Set-level coverage mixes within-person and across-person variety. The paper contrasts this broader design space at total idea level with homogenization at image level (p. 11, Section 5.1).

eligibility.reason: Four student groups were randomly assigned to sketching (n=31) or free generative-AI use (n=30) (p. 4, Section 3.2.2); 61 students' outputs were rated, above the 50-person threshold; creativity was rated by three experts on the outputs (p. 4, Section 3.2.3; p. 6). Caveat for review: randomization was of only four intact groups (two clusters per arm), not individuals, and all reported tests treat ideas as independent.

one_line_finding: Expert CAT ratings of image-level ideas averaged 2.89 for AI groups vs 2.52 for sketch groups (p. 6, Table 1), with a significant difference in one group pair (2.94 vs 2.36, t(76) = -3.995, p < .001) and none in the other (2.82 vs 3.04, p = .306); AI students produced more total ideas (9.7 vs 2.8 per participant) but fewer image-level ideas (1.4 vs 2.2), and 18 of 30 AI students converged on one concept (pp. 6-7).
open_questions: Group labels conflict: Methods (p. 4, Section 3.2.2) and Figure 1 (p. 3) say sketch = groups A+C and AI = groups B+D, but the t-tests in Section 4.2.1 (p. 6) label Group A and Group B as Sketch and Group C and Group D as AI. The idea counts (54+17 = 71 sketch, 24+20 = 44 AI) match the Section 4.2.1 labels.

The reported d = 0.60 with 95% CI [-0.98, -0.47] (p. 6) looks inconsistent: the printed means differ by 0.58 on SDs near 0.6, and the interval has the opposite sign to d and resembles a CI for the mean difference. An extractor should not use this d without checking.
Number of students per group (A, B, C, D) is not given, only per condition (31 and 30).
Design class: the session ran inside a regular mandatory course workshop (p. 3, Section 3.1), coded field_rct; it could also be read as lab_rct (supervised session).
notes: Outcomes not listed: the Alternative Uses Test (Top2 scoring, three professors, Cronbach's alpha 0.65; M = 2.8, SD = 0.51) was a baseline diagnostic before assignment, and its Pearson correlations with design-task fluency (sketch r=.12, p=.54; AI r=.08, p=.67) and creativity (sketch r=.12, p=.53; AI r=-.30, p=.103) are not AI effects (pp. 5 and 7, Sections 4.1 and 4.2.4). The exit survey (p. 10, Section 4.3) and the diagnostic questionnaire (42 respondents) are self-reports. The exploration-path coding (Figure 6) and the thematic prompt analysis (27 of 30 AI logs, Table 2) describe process, not scored outputs. The paper calls itself an exploratory study; the sketch arm had no access to any other stimulus (p. 12, Section 5.4). Funding not stated.
